title: Demi-Glace
description: Deep, rich, concentrated beef sauce. Makes about 2-3 litres.

ingredients.notes: knuckle, marrow, or oxtail - ask your butcher
rough chop, skin on for colour
or enough to cover bones by 5cm
Don't add too much all at once — you can't take it out once it's in.

youWillNeed.note: Commercial base - mixed to a thick paste - follow directions on pack.

method.instruction: Preheat oven to 200°C. Roast beef bones and scraps on a tray until deeply browned - about 45 minutes. Don't rush this. Brown equals flavour.
Transfer roasted bones and scraps to your stockpot. Add onion, carrot, celery, bay leaves, and peppercorns.
Cover with 4 litres of cold water. Bring to a simmer - not a rolling boil. Skim foam off the top regularly.
Simmer gently for 6-8 hours. Top up with water if bones become exposed. Low and slow wins here.
Strain stock through a fine mesh strainer lined with cheesecloth into a clean pot. Discard solids.
Return stock to heat. Simmer and reduce until you have about 2-3 litres of concentrated, silky liquid - roughly 1-2 more hours.

Mix demi-glace powder with a small amount of cold water to form a smooth, thick paste. Whisk into hot stock until dissolved. Start with about 50g powder per litre and adjust. You can always add more. You cannot take it back.
Taste. Add a pinch of salt if needed. Remember: this will concentrate further when used in other dishes.
Pour into storage containers. Leave headspace. Cool slightly before refrigerating.
Refrigerate overnight. Fat will rise and solidify. Skim it off completely and discard.
Use within 1 week, or freeze for up to 3 months. Portion into smaller containers for easy grabbing.

notes.title: The Powder Ratio
notes.content: Start with 50g demi-glace powder per 1 litre of reduced stock. Mix to a paste first. Whisk in. Simmer 5 minutes. Taste. Add more if you want it thicker or richer. The right consistency should coat the back of a spoon like slow velvet.

notes.title: Skim That Fat
notes.content: After a night in the fridge, the fat cap will be solid. Peel it off. Throw it away. That fat is not flavour - it's just bone grease. Your sauce should be silky, not oily.

notes.title: Chef's Note
notes.content: Demi-glace is what separates bistro cooking from home cooking. You don't need much - a ladleful transforms a pan sauce. Make a batch. Freeze it in portions. Thank yourself later.
